quote_text: There is no absurdity so palpable but that it may be firmly planted in the human head if you only begin to inculcate it before the age of five.
idea_text: Doorstep dread — the certainty, arriving about ninety seconds after you leave, that you left the stove on.
Spoilerdrift — when a streaming app's episode list quietly tells you a character survives to season four.
Toogoodhoard — the pile of things you cannot use and refuse to throw out because someone, somewhere, would want them.
Photo lag — the four days between a trip ending and the one friend who took the good pictures sending them.
Tab guilt — the specific weight of forty open browser tabs you are keeping because closing one admits you will never read it.
The overtake — accelerating slightly to pass a slow walker before the corner, for no reason and no prize.
Queue faith — the moment you commit to a checkout line and refuse to switch even as the other one empties.
App sprawl — the six workplace tools that each do one ninth of a job and none of which anyone chose.
Recess hunger — the mid-afternoon office feeling that what you actually need is fifteen minutes on a climbing frame.
Lift limbo — the silence between floors when two colleagues have already said everything they are willing to say.

quote_text: When stress is the problem, slack is the solution.
idea_text: Pick one café and go at the same time three days running, until they start the order before you say it.
Learn the route between two places well enough to walk it without your phone out. One route is enough to stop feeling lost.
Buy something that needs repairing later — shoes, a watch strap, a kettle. Now you have a reason to find the repair man, who knows everyone.
Eat the thing the city is embarrassed about rather than the thing it is famous for.
Find the one park bench with the best view and go back to it at a different hour.
Ask the person at the counter where they eat on their day off, then actually go.
Get on a bus with no destination and get off when it looks interesting. You will learn the shape of the place faster than any map.
Introduce yourself to exactly one neighbour before you have a reason to.
Find where the city is quiet in the middle of the day — a library reading room, an empty temple, a cinema at 2pm.
Take a photograph from the same spot on day one and day seven. The second one will be of a place you know.
